lessons.title: Standards and work instructions
lessons.html:
Standards and work instructions

Controlling practices means making sure every operation in the orchard or vineyard is done to the right standard, at the right time, safely and within budget. This practical module covers how the foreman sets standards, checks the work and corrects problems.

Where standards come from

  • The farm's technical consultant: pruning bud loads, thinning spacing, canopy targets, spray programmes.
  • Product labels: rates, withholding and re-entry periods, PPE.
  • Market and food safety requirements: hygiene, traceability, residue limits.
  • Farm policies and the OHS Act 85 of 1993: safe work procedures.

Writing work instructions

For each major operation, prepare a short work instruction that workers and team leaders can follow:

  1. What the operation is and why it is done.
  2. The standard - in numbers where possible (buds per spur, fruit per cluster, cm between fruit, shoots per metre).
  3. The method, step by step.
  4. Tools and PPE.
  5. Safety and hygiene rules.
  6. How the work will be checked.

Keep instructions simple, in the language the team uses, and with pictures or demonstration where possible.

Before the operation starts

Hold a demonstration in the block: show a correctly done tree or vine and a few common mistakes. Let each worker do a tree while you or the team leader watch. Only then let the team work at full speed. Mark a demonstration tree at the start of a row as a reference.

Timing

Many practices have narrow windows: chemical thinning at a fruitlet size, shoot thinning before shoots harden, sprays before rain. Monitor crop stage daily and start operations on time; late work costs more and achieves less.

lessons.title: Inspecting and correcting the work
lessons.html:
Inspecting and correcting the work

Systematic inspection

Check work while it is happening, not only after the block is finished. Use a sampling plan: for example, check a set number of trees per worker per day, or every tenth tree in a row. Record the results on a quality sheet.

OperationWhat to check
PruningBud or spur numbers, cut quality, correct wood removed
ThinningFruit count and spacing, damaged fruit removed
Canopy workShoot numbers, positioning, leaf removal level
SprayingCalibration, coverage, correct product and rate, records
IrrigationEmitters working, pressure, soil moisture
PickingMaturity, damage, bin filling, hygiene

Correcting problems

  • Correct immediately and in the row, so the worker can see the problem and fix it.
  • Find the root cause: unclear instruction, blunt tools, poor training, rushing because of the incentive system, fatigue.
  • Fix the cause, not only the tree: retrain, replace tools, adjust the incentive to include quality.
  • Have badly done sections redone where it is still possible.
  • Record what was found and done.

Spray application control

Spraying needs special control because mistakes can cause crop loss or residue violations. Check that the right product and rate are in the tank against the spray instruction, that the sprayer is calibrated, that weather conditions are suitable, that the operator wears PPE, and that the spray record is completed with withholding and re-entry dates. Post re-entry warnings at the block and prevent workers from entering too early.

Safety checks

During inspections, also check safety: ladders used correctly, PPE worn, tractors driven slowly near workers, water and shade available. Stop unsafe work immediately.

lessons.title: Records, compliance and continuous improvement
lessons.html:
Records, compliance and continuous improvement

Records that prove control

Records show that practices were done correctly. They are required for food safety and sustainability audits and help the farm learn from each season. Key records include:

  • Spray records: date, block, product, rate, volume, operator, weather, withholding and re-entry dates.
  • Fertiliser and irrigation records per block.
  • Scouting records and decisions taken.
  • Quality inspection sheets per operation.
  • Training and induction registers.
  • Hygiene checks of toilets and handwashing facilities during harvest.
  • Incident and injury reports.

Audits

Export farms are audited against food safety and social standards. Auditors check that records exist, are complete, and match what they see in the field and stores. Keep records up to date daily; reconstructing them afterwards is unreliable and may be seen as falsification.

Legal compliance

Use only registered agricultural remedies according to label under Act 36 of 1947. Store chemicals safely. Respect water allocations under the National Water Act 36 of 1998. Protect soil under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983. Meet labour and safety laws.

Continuous improvement

After each operation, review with team leaders:

  1. Did we meet the standard? What percentage of samples passed?
  2. Did we finish on time and within budget?
  3. What went wrong and why?
  4. What will we do differently next time?

At the end of the season, compare quality records with packout and yield per block. This shows which practices made the biggest difference and where training should focus.

Reporting

Report to the manager on completion, quality results, problems and corrective actions, and any compliance concerns.

Key points

  • Base standards on consultant advice, labels, market rules and safety law.
  • Use clear work instructions and demonstrations before work starts.
  • Inspect by sampling during the work and correct immediately.
  • Control spraying tightly: product, rate, calibration, PPE, records, re-entry.
  • Keep daily records for audits and use them to improve.

While the work is happening, using a sampling plan

quiz.question: Why mark a demonstration tree at the start of a row?

options.text: As a reference of the correct standard
To show where the toilet is

options.text: Adjusting the incentive to include quality

options.text: It is faster to remember later
